meta.name: Spanish Water Dog
meta.tagline: The Spanish Water Dog is a rustic, athletic working breed with a distinctive corded coat that should never be brushed. Versatile across herding, hunting, and water work, they're intensely loyal to their family and reserved with everyone else.
meta.excerpt: The Spanish Water Dog is a genuine working breed — used for herding, hunting, and water retrieval across Spain for centuries. Their curly coat forms natural cords and should never be brushed. They're athletic, devoted to their family, and reserved with strangers. Not a beginner breed.
meta.meta_description: Spanish Water Dog breed guide: the no-brush corded coat explained, temperament with family and strangers, health screening requirements, and whether this versatile herding breed fits your life.

intro.label: Overview
intro.heading: What Is a Spanish Water Dog?
intro.html:
The Spanish Water Dog — Perro de Agua Español in its home country — is an ancient breed from the Iberian Peninsula with a working history that spans herding sheep and goats, retrieving game from water, and assisting fishermen along the Andalusian coast. This is a dog bred for actual work across multiple disciplines, not a breed developed for the show ring. That heritage shapes everything about them: their physicality, their intelligence, their intensity, and their loyalty.

The breed's most immediately distinctive feature is the coat — a curly, woolly single coat that either cords naturally over time or is kept clipped short. It should never be brushed. Brushing destroys the coat texture permanently, breaks up the natural cord formation, and results in a frizzy, structurally compromised coat that no longer serves its intended function. This is one of the most non-negotiable breed facts in the dog world.

The Spanish Water Dog was recognized by the AKC in 2015. It remains relatively uncommon in the United States, which means finding a health-testing breeder requires research — but the reward is a breed that is genuinely unlike the typical herding dog experience.

appearance.label: Physical
appearance.heading: What Spanish Water Dogs Look Like
appearance.html:
Medium-sized and solidly built — males typically 40–49 lbs and 17.75–19.75 inches at the shoulder; females 31–40 lbs and 15.75–18 inches. The body is slightly longer than tall, with the muscular, athletic build of a dog designed to work all day across varied terrain. The face is broad, with almond-shaped eyes in hazel to chestnut brown and pendant ears that hang flat against the head.

The coat is the breed's most defining characteristic. It is a single-layer curly coat — there is no undercoat — that forms natural cords as it grows. Coat colors include solid black, brown, beige, white, and parti-color combinations. When clipped, the dog has a clean, low-maintenance appearance. When corded, the locks hang in tight, ropelike cords. Both expressions are correct; both require a specific approach to maintenance that does not involve brushing.

temperament.label: Personality
temperament.heading: Temperament
temperament.html:
With family: deeply loyal and bonded. Spanish Water Dogs are not dogs that distribute their affection broadly — they choose their people and commit fully. This is a breed that wants to be with you, work with you, and know exactly where you are at all times. In a household that understands this quality, it reads as devotion. In a household that isn't prepared for it, it can manifest as separation anxiety or velcro-dog behavior.

With strangers: distinctly reserved. Spanish Water Dogs are not unfriendly, but they are not particularly welcoming either. A well-socialized specimen will be politely neutral — watchful, controlled, not approaching for attention. An under-socialized one will be reactive and difficult to manage in public situations. Early, consistent socialization is not optional for this breed.

With other dogs: generally manageable with proper socialization, though the breed's working-dog intensity means introductions should be deliberate. Spanish Water Dogs raised with other dogs from puppyhood typically coexist well. Adding an unfamiliar adult dog to the household requires the standard careful introduction protocols.

mikes_take.label: A Realistic Take
mikes_take.heading: What I'd Tell a Friend Thinking About a Spanish Water Dog
mikes_take.html:
The Spanish Water Dog is genuinely interesting — an authentic multi-purpose working breed with a coat system unlike anything else in the herding group, a loyal and athletic temperament, and a relative rarity that means the people who seek them out tend to be serious. If you do agility, herding trials, nosework, or dock diving, this breed is worth your serious attention. They're capable of excelling at all of it.

The honest conversation starts with the coat. You need to be genuinely committed to either learning how to maintain cords properly — a time-consuming practice, especially in the early stages — or clipping the coat short every few months. What you cannot do is brush it. If your instinct is to pick up a brush whenever you see a curly-coated dog, this is the breed that will train that instinct out of you.

The second conversation is about exercise and engagement. This is a high-drive working breed. Daily structured exercise plus mental stimulation is the minimum — a Spanish Water Dog left under-stimulated will find work to do, and it won't be the work you want done. For the right active household, they are wonderful. For a quieter household looking for a calm companion, look elsewhere.

care.label: Daily Life
care.heading: Care Requirements
care.html:
Exercise

60–90 minutes of vigorous daily exercise. This is a working dog built for endurance, not a breed that can be maintained on short neighborhood walks. Hiking, swimming, fetch, agility, herding — all are appropriate. Mental stimulation through training, puzzle work, or a dog sport is equally important for this intelligent breed.

Coat Care

The Spanish Water Dog coat is maintained in one of two ways: corded or clipped. Never brush the coat. Brushing permanently damages the texture and prevents proper cord formation. If keeping the coat in cords: allow the curls to begin forming naturally, then separate cords manually as needed to prevent matting from the base — never brush, only separate with fingers. If keeping the coat clipped: clip every 2–3 months, keeping the coat at a uniform length. See the Spanish Water Dog grooming guide for the full approach.

Training

Intelligent and willing, but with the independent streak of a breed that was developed to make decisions without constant handler direction. Positive reinforcement training works well. Early obedience, followed by a dog sport or structured activity, gives the brain the outlet it needs. These dogs learn quickly and retain well — the challenge is keeping training interesting rather than repetitive.

health.label: Wellness
health.heading: Health & Common Conditions
health.html:
The Spanish Water Dog is generally a hardy working breed with a 12–14 year lifespan. As a relatively rare breed, the gene pool requires careful stewardship, and reputable breeders invest in comprehensive health testing. Two conditions require DNA testing before purchase.

ConditionWhat It Means
Hip DysplasiaMalformed hip joint leading to arthritis and pain. OFA or PennHIP screening required; ask for parental clearances. Manageable medically in mild-moderate cases; severe cases may require surgery.
Progressive Retinal Atrophy (PRA)Inherited retinal degeneration leading to progressive vision loss and blindness. DNA test available — reputable breeders test both parents. No treatment. Ask your breeder for DNA test clearances for both parents.
HypothyroidismUnderactive thyroid gland causing weight gain, lethargy, and skin/coat changes. Manageable with daily medication once diagnosed. OFA thyroid clearance available from breeders.
GlaucomaIncreased intraocular pressure that can lead to permanent blindness if untreated. Can be primary (inherited) or secondary. CAER eye exam can identify affected dogs. Seek immediate veterinary attention for any sudden eye pain, redness, or cloudiness.

Ask breeders for: OFA hip clearance, PRA DNA test, OFA thyroid clearance, and CAER eye exam for both parents.

right_for_you.label: Fit Assessment
right_for_you.heading: Is a Spanish Water Dog Right for You?
good_fit: Active owners who hike, swim, or participate in dog sports (agility, herding, nosework, dock diving)
Households committed to learning the no-brush coat care system
Owners who want a deeply loyal, one-family dog with strong working drive
Experienced owners who understand reserved, independent-minded herding breeds
Committed to early and thorough socialization to manage stranger reserve
not_fit: First-time dog owners without prior herding or working breed experience
Owners looking for a social, everyone-is-a-friend type of dog
Anyone who cannot commit to 60–90 minutes of daily vigorous exercise
Households expecting to brush the dog's curly coat (this permanently damages the coat)
Low-activity households where mental and physical stimulation is limited

finding.label: Next Steps
finding.heading: Finding Your Spanish Water Dog
finding.html:
Buying from a Breeder

$1,500–$2,500 from reputable breeders. The breed is uncommon in the US, so expect a waitlist from quality breeders. Required health clearances: OFA hip evaluation, PRA DNA test for both parents, OFA thyroid clearance, and CAER eye exam. The Spanish Water Dog Club of America maintains breeder referrals. Do not purchase from breeders who cannot produce DNA test documentation.

Rescue

Spanish Water Dogs are rare enough in the US that breed-specific rescue is limited. General herding breed rescues occasionally have them. Patience is required. Adult rescues of this breed work best with experienced herding-breed owners who can provide structure and an appropriate activity outlet.

Before your Spanish Water Dog comes home, complete the Spanish Water Dog puppy checklist — socialization planning and coat care decisions (cord vs. clip) are the two things to work through before the puppy arrives.

faq.q: Can you brush a Spanish Water Dog's coat?
faq.a: No — and this is one of the most critical breed-specific facts. The Spanish Water Dog's curly single coat forms natural cords over time. Brushing destroys the texture permanently, creates frizz, and prevents proper cord formation. The coat is maintained either by allowing cords to form (separating them manually at the base with fingers, never a brush) or by clipping it short periodically. If you find yourself wanting to brush a curly coat, this breed will require a genuine change in approach.

faq.q: Are Spanish Water Dogs good family dogs?
faq.a: Yes, for the right family — one that is active, experienced with working breeds, and committed to early socialization. Spanish Water Dogs are deeply loyal to their own household, including children they grow up with. They are not broadly social dogs and will be reserved with visitors and strangers. They require real daily exercise. For an active family prepared for these qualities, they are excellent dogs.

faq.q: How much exercise does a Spanish Water Dog need?
faq.a: 60–90 minutes of vigorous daily exercise minimum, plus mental engagement through training or a dog sport. This is a working dog with genuine endurance built for all-day field work. A Spanish Water Dog that doesn't get adequate exercise and mental stimulation will redirect that energy into problem behaviors. Dog sports — agility, herding, nosework, dock diving — are ideal outlets.

faq.q: What health tests should Spanish Water Dog breeders perform?
faq.a: OFA hip evaluation, PRA (Progressive Retinal Atrophy) DNA test for both parents, OFA thyroid clearance, and CAER eye exam. PRA is particularly important — it is an inherited condition with a DNA test available, and a reputable breeder will have documentation for both parents. Walk away from any breeder who cannot provide these clearances.
